cards.issue: Specific written landlord consent for sub-letting under Section 14(1)(b)
cards.proposition: The Court held that the statutory consent must be the landlord's written consent to the specific sub-letting. A general lease clause permitting assignment or parting with possession to unspecified 'associate concerns' without further consent did not satisfy that requirement for the later induction of M/s United Automobiles.

conditions.textual_justification: The Court contrasted the lease's general wording with the required specific consent.

cards.effect: The general associate-concern clause could not save the tenant, even assuming the clause was admissible and the sub-lessee was an associate concern.
exceptions_limitations: The Court did not need to decide whether United Automobiles actually qualified as an 'associate concern' for this alternative holding.
Landlord consent is distinct from permission granted by a tenant to an occupant.
Dealer, distributor, associate concern, licensee, tenant, and sub-tenant must remain separate source states unless the judgment establishes a relation.

cards.issue: Late factual plea of permissive possession at the special-leave stage
cards.proposition: The Court refused to entertain the appellants' new factual plea that the tenant-father had permitted his sons to occupy half the shop because the plea had not been taken in the written statement or pressed below, was inconsistent with the earlier plea that the father possessed the entire premises, and would deny the respondent an opportunity to rebut it and likely cause prejudice. The Court also stated that permissive possession cannot be presumed merely from father-son relationship, joint living, or joint messing.

cards.issue: Reliance on a sub-letting-permission clause contained in an unregistered lease deed
cards.proposition: The Court held that whether a lessee may create a sub-lease is a term of the lease transaction. If the lease document is inadmissible for non-registration, the permission-to-sublet term cannot be detached and proved separately as collateral; the tenant therefore could not rely on that clause.

scope.legislation_provision: Registration issue discussed with reference to Section 49 of the Registration Act by the parties; complete statutory text is not supplied
scope.historical_date: Judgment dated 1989-08-08; lease deed executed in 1961
scope.procedural_stage: Supreme Court appeal in eviction proceeding
scope.document_scope: The unregistered lease deed and its sub-letting-permission clause in this case

conditions.textual_justification: The Court said this question is a term of the lease transaction and cannot be disassociated.

evidence.quote: The question whether a lessee is entitled to create a sub-lease, or not is undoubtedly a term of the transaction of lease

conditions.condition: If D is inadmissible for non-registration, C is inadmissible with the other terms and cannot be relied on.
conditions.textual_justification: The Court expressly included the landlord-permission term within the inadmissible terms.

evidence.quote: If a document is inad- missible for non-registration, all its terms are inadmissi- ble including the one dealing with landlord's permission to his tenant to sub-let.

cards.effect: The appellant could not rely on the associate-concern permission clause in its unregistered lease deed.
exceptions_limitations: The attachment does not provide the complete Registration Act or all exceptions; this card is limited to the lease-term issue actually decided.
The Court also gave an independent alternative reason: the lease clause was general and did not amount to specific written consent.
This rule concerns admissibility of a lease term, not whether United Automobiles had physical use or legal possession.

law_segments.text: A perusal of its language would show that it contains the respondent's consent in general terms without reference to M/s. United Automobiles. As a matter of fact M/s. United Automobiles came to be inducted as a sub-tenant much later. Can such a general permission be treated to be the consent as required by S. 14 (1) Proviso (b) of the Act? It was held by this Court In M/s. Shalimar Tar Products v. S.C. Sharma, [1988] 1 SCC 70; that Ss.

14(1) Proviso (b) and 16(2) and (3) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 enjoin the tenant to obtain consent of the landlord in writing to the specific sub-letting and any other interpretation of the provisions will defeat the object of the statute and is, therefore, inpermissible. Since it is not suggested that the consent of the respondent was obtained specifically with reference to the Sub-letting in favour of M/s. United Automobiles, the clause in the lease deed, which has been relied on can not save the appellant, even if it be assumed in its favour that the clause is admissible and the sUb-lessee is appel- lant's associate concern.

It has been taken for the first time in the special leave petition. The plea is inconsistent with the plea taken in the written statement. In the written statement, the plea, in substance, was that the first appellant was in possession over the entire accommodation. The plea now sought to be raised is that the second and third appellants were in possession of the half portion of the shop exclusively but with his permission. The new plea is not a pleading of law; it is a pleading of fact. The respondent had no opportunity of confuting the plea. If we allow the appellants to take the new plea now, it is likely to cause him prejudice. 6.

No presumption can be drawn from mere relationship of the father and son or from joint living and joint messing that the second and third appellants were' in permissive possession of the half portion. If the appellants had taken this plea in their written statement, the respondent would have got an opportunity of proving that the plea was false. 7. Having regard to these circumstances, we are not permitting the appellants to raise the new plea. It is now too late. 8. There is no force in this appeal and accordingly it is dismissed. In the circumstances of this case, there will be no order as to costs. Dr. Vijay Kumar And Ors. vs Raghbir Singh Anokh Singh on 22 May, 1973

registration, none of the terms of the lease can be admitted in evidence and that to use a document for the purpose of proving an important clause in the lease is not using it as a collateral purpose. 8. The learned counsel for the appellant attempted to meet the point by saying that so far the consent of the landlord permitting sub-letting is concerned, it does not require registration and the clause, therefore, must be excepted from the requirement of registration and consequent exclusion from evidence. We do not see any force in this argument.

The question whether a lessee is entitled to create a sub-lease, or not is undoubtedly a term of the transaction of lease, and if it is incorporated in the document it can not be disassociated from the lease and considered separately in isolation. If a document is inad- missible for non-registration, all its terms are inadmissi- ble including the one dealing with landlord's permission to his tenant to sub-let. It follows that the appellant can not, in the present circumstances, be allowed to rely upon the clause in his unregistered lease deed. 9. There is still another reason to hold that the afore- said clause can not come to the aid of the appellant.
